units.translation: I see this crowd of the gods of the assembly, shaded by freshly plucked branches, bowing down (thus Hermann for τῶνδ᾽ [of these]). The scholiast correctly: "I see a crowd of gods crowned with suppliant branches." What is read in M as νέον θ᾽ [new and] Bamberger emended by restoring νεύονθ᾽ [bowing]. τόνδ᾽ [this] which Hermann wrote is more probable than τῶνδ᾽ [of these], which is correctly read at v. 332: τί φὴς ἱκνείσθαι τῶνδ᾽ ἀγωνίων θεῶν, λευκοστεφεῖς ἔχουσα νεοδρέπτους κλάδους [Why do you say you come as suppliant of these gods of the assembly, holding white-crowned, freshly plucked branches?], where the suppliants are said to hold branches in their hands, but in the other passage the gods are shaded by branches, after the suppliants have placed the branches on the statues of the gods. "But the branches are not to be understood as nodding, but the gods as showing, by being adorned with branches, that it is impious to reject suppliants." Hermann.
the crowd bowing to these gods of the assembly
ναύειν [to supplicate]: to supplicate, from the fact that suppliants flee to the hearth. ναύω [I supplicate]: I entreat, I supplicate
ναύειν [to supplicate]: to supplicate, since they were in temples, or at the hearth, from ἐναῦσαι [to kindle]. crowd
of these gods of the assembly
the crowd bowing to these gods of the assembly
the crowd supplicating the gods of the assembly
bringing this sailor as a suppliant at the hearth of the gods
ναύει [it flows]: it flows, it gushes
holding a cloud over him. Thus Casaubon for ὑποσχών [holding under].
and watery clouds, where, after removing the gloss, I restored κύφελλ᾽ ὑδρηλά [watery clouds], about which I spoke under this word.
It is an Attic form, of which there are no examples in Sophocles and Euripides, who often used the common ναός [temple], of which in turn there is no example in Aeschylus.
they did not hesitate to plunder the statues of the gods nor to burn the temples.
a new belly self-sufficient in children
wasting away with vapor, with fire in the belly
nor raised in the darkness of the belly
he will strike you with dung, with the juices of the belly

In M νηΐστησι [Neistai], with the first part of the letter stigma erased: hence νηΐτησι [Neitai] in the copies. Heathius proposed Νηΐταισι [Neitai]. In the same way it varies in other writers, and the origin of the name is not sufficiently certain (about which Pausanias 9, 8, 4 spoke). See Unger's Thebana Paradoxa p. 311 and Thesaurus vol. 5 p. 1482.
to attack the company at the Neistai gates
but pitilessly (in many copies ἀλλ᾽ ἀνηλεῶς [but mercilessly]) thus I have been disciplined
